TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
WEDNESDAY, 27 MAY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 2, DAY 3
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC, COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH ZELIE HEGER SC AND
ELEANOR JONES AND JOE PETRY AND DAVID ROWE, COUNSEL
ASSISTING

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.01 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Yes, Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Commissioner, could I begin with the tender of the
statements and associated documents from yesterday's hearing. The team has
prepared a list.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: In the now usual way, I won't specify each of those but
I tender the documents.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, very well. The documents are received and will be
marked in accordance with that index list that you have supplied and to which I take
it the parties have access, Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, I asked for that process to be put in place so I assume
it has been.
COMMISSIONER: I'm seeing vigorous nods from the bar table.
MS CALLAN SC: I'm not sure about that, Commissioner, but I'm sure we'll get
access at an appropriate time. I just wanted to confirm, in respect of Assistant
Commissioner Cook's statement, you may recall when he indicated it was true and
correct at a general level, he identified there had been some correspondence which
corrected, I think, mainly some cross-references. That was conveyed in a letter to the
Commission dated 22 May 2026. As long as that letter forms part of the tender, then,
for the record, that will make it clear.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. No, the corrected of the form of the statement is the
one that is tendered.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. I shouldn't have said vigorous nods, Ms Callan. I didn't
for a moment think it was assent. I thought it was rather the opposite from yourself
and Ms Munro, and I understand that administrative arrangements are being put in
place. It's simply that we take up the first half-hour of the session with me reading
exhibit numbers, getting them wrong and being corrected by Mr Lancaster. So if the
both of you are content with that, it will be attended to in the course of the day.
MS CALLAN SC: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Thanks, Mr Lancaster.
MR LANCASTER SC: I call Deputy Commissioner Hudson.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.

<DAVID WILLIAM HUDSON, CALLED
COMMISSIONER: Yes, take a seat. Thank you, Deputy Commissioner.
MR LANCASTER SC: Please state your full name.
DC HUDSON: My full name is David William Hudson, H-u-d-s-o-n.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your address is known to the Commission. And you have
prepared a statement 23 April 2026?
DC HUDSON: Yes, I have, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Are the contents of that statement true and correct to the
best of your knowledge and belief?
DC HUDSON: Yes, they are.
MR LANCASTER SC: That will be tendered in due course, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You are Deputy Commissioner of Investigations and
Counter Terrorism since 2017.
DC HUDSON: Correct, sir, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have strategic responsibility for a number of
commands under the New South Wales Police Force, including the State Crime
Command?
DC HUDSON: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Counter Terrorism & Special Tactics Command?
DC HUDSON: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: The Police Prosecutions and Licensing Enforcement
Command, which includes the Firearms Registry?
DC HUDSON: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the State Intelligence Command?
DC HUDSON: Correct.

MR LANCASTER SC: Among a couple of others.
DC HUDSON: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I first ask you about the section of your statement
where you address funding. As with other officers who have provided statements,
thank you for the written response to these questions asked by the Commission.
Question 5 asked about funding, particularly of the counter terrorism function. You
indicate in paragraph 18 that the police did not specifically seek any funding increase
between 7 October 2023 and 14 December 2025 but that was because you considered
funding resources allocated to counter terrorism was sufficient in that period. Is that
your evidence?
DC HUDSON: That's correct, sir. Yes, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: You refer to CTSC, which is the Counter Terrorism
Command, benefitting from an increase over the last five years or so.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Has that been a year-on-year increase or could you describe
how that has changed?
DC HUDSON: Sir, since I came into my position, they've had increase in
resourcing. In 2017 or 2018, sorry, there was an allocation of 1500 officers to the
New South Wales Police Force by the government. They were allocated based on
a needs-basis, and Counter Terrorism & Special Tactics Command did receive
resources out of those allocations, plus there were additional units attached in that
period to the Counter Terrorism Command, including what was initially the Fixated
Persons Unit but we subsequently renamed that to the Security Investigations Unit
and the Terrorism High Risk Offenders Unit once the legislation had passed by
government.
Plus some incremental increases in relation to movement of commands within
Counter Terrorism. The Security Management Unit was allocated somewhere else,
but two years ago we moved it back into Counter Terrorism so that was another 200
officers that entered the command.
MR LANCASTER SC: Were you referring there to the last five-year period or was
that the period immediately after you commenced?
DC HUDSON: It was around the same time. I think Fixated Persons Unit came in
2017, but subsequently changed names and was fully integrated into the Counter
Terrorism Command. Then the Terrorism High Risk Offenders Unit, I think, was
around 2018 as well. But apart from those additions to capability within the
command, there's been incremental increases in a number of units based on needs
and allocations out of that 1500 personnel.

MR LANCASTER SC: Did police identify a need of that sort after the 7 October
2023 Hamas attack in respect of its counter terrorism work in New South Wales?
DC HUDSON: It wasn't considered that Counter Terrorism Command needed
additional resources. It was supplemented by Operation Shelter. Some of the work
undertaken by that unit that was split up in October of 2023 to - in a surge capacity in
relation to overcoming what was identified at that time as to what the need was.
MR LANCASTER SC: And the surge capacity would draw on officers from other
commands? Or how does the surge capacity work in practice?
DC HUDSON: Yes, it draws from other commands. There's a model built about
what numbers are required and then that is supplemented through a staffing order
that is either done through secondments from other commands or on a shift-by-shift
basis.
MR LANCASTER SC: But you have been satisfied yourself that over the last five
years, there has been sufficient funding and resources allocated to counter terrorism
efforts in the state?
DC HUDSON: Yes, I am, sir. When the threat level was downgraded, we didn't
reduce our capability, and subsequently when it was increased, we didn't have a need
for additional resources because we hadn't downgraded the Counter Terrorism
Command with that downgraded threat level.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thank you. Part of your responsibilities that you've
described in paragraph 10 are:
"Developing operational strategies, plans and guidelines for effective and efficient
policing operations."
It's what you refer to in 10(a), among other things. And then in 10(b), among the
responsibilities you identify there are:
"The development and implementation of strategies and plans to build response and
capability within the force."
DC HUDSON: That's correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you about one aspect of that, which is risk - risk
and threat assessment procedures. The Commission heard yesterday that in 2025
there was no guideline or policy in place that was provided or available to an
operations inspector to assist them in making risk and threat assessments in respect
of decisions about the allocation of police resources to community events within
a police area command at the local level. Can I ask you, do you agree it's important
to have a consistent, predictable and thorough approach to making risk or threat

assessments for that purpose? In other words, at the local level by an operations
inspector who just is day-to-day dealing with assessing the risk of a community
event that's upcoming?
DC HUDSON: The responsibilities I have are particular to the commands that sit
under me. I believe that each region has their own process of risk and threat
assessment, but I do agree there should be some consistency in that process. I think
the organisation will look at that.
MR LANCASTER SC: In your view, would a guideline or even a checklist of
considerations be a useful resource for operations inspector or inspectors or PAC
commanders making those sorts of decisions about allocation of resources for
upcoming community events?
DC HUDSON: A process or policy or guideline as you have suggested, sir, would
certainly get consistency in the outcome.
MR LANCASTER SC: It would also perhaps avoid the risk of busy operations
inspectors or PAC commanders - and I'm not referring particularly to the eastern
suburbs; I'm referring generally to operations inspectors and PAC commanders. But
a guideline or at least a checklist would ensure that consideration is given to all
necessary considerations before these important decisions about police allocation of
resources is made; do you agree?
DC HUDSON: I don't disagree, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you about Strike Force Pearl, which you address
in one section of your statement. That was established on 13 December 2024 to
investigate antisemitic grievance-based offences in Sydney?
DC HUDSON: Correct.
MR LANCASTER SC: How was that resourced and staffed?
DC HUDSON: Initially, it was resourced through the Security Investigations Unit,
their staff, and Central Metropolitan Region staff under the leadership of a Security
Investigations Inspector.
MR LANCASTER SC: You've referred in paragraph 48 of your statement to its
high-visibility taskings and its intelligence work, haven't you?
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I just ask you to look in the middle of that paragraph.
You refer to Operation Talon style taskings see where you've mentioned that
description.

DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you explain what you mean by that sort of tasking?
DC HUDSON: Operation Talon was an operation designed in 2013 in response to
the organised crime environment of escalated shootings and violence on our streets.
In essence, it was a saturation-type operation where identified individuals who were
known to us - whether they had a firearms prohibition order may have been checked
along that process as well. That became - it was a surge capability at the time for
Talon, to overcome a specific need at the time but has been a model that has been
utilised on different occasions subsequently.
MR LANCASTER SC: But those kind of processes were picked up and applied by
Strike Force Pearl when it had dedicated staffing?
DC HUDSON: High-visibility operations, engagement with the community,
engagement with individuals of interest to us.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have indicated in paragraph 51 that Strike Force Pearl
is no longer operating as a standalone strike force, with dedicated staffing. So has
there been some replacement function or operation to take its place?
DC HUDSON: Sir, Pearl was created for a specific reason with a specific terms of
reference, to - in response to an escalation in violent behaviour in the eastern suburbs
of firebombings and graffiti that were almost exclusively targeting the Jewish
community. There were a number of arrests made in March of 2025. As a result of
those arrests, the incidents of that nature disappeared, and whilst there are
investigations ongoing in relation to a couple of those incidents and court matters
being put before the courts, those responsibilities have been absorbed back to the
main investigators rather than standalone strike force.
MR LANCASTER SC: The structure of Pearl seems to involve - and correct me if I
am wrong, but it involved a combination of those high visibility taskings on the one
hand but with very close relationship with other members of that team who were
analysts and intelligence analysts; is that right?
DC HUDSON: And detectives.
MR LANCASTER SC: And detectives. So is that model of a centralised group of
intelligence officers, analysts, detectives and high visibility policing something the
police regard as a particularly effective way of dealing with antisemitic violence and
crime?
DC HUDSON: The responsibilities for Pearl are transferred to Operation Shelter,
which was the high visibility operation that we commenced on 11 October 2023,
shortly after the Hamas terrorist attack. So those taskings and high visibility
operations were transferred, once Pearl had disbanded, to Operation Shelter.

MR LANCASTER SC: So the Operation Shelter model was similar to what you've
described as the Operation Talon style tasking and Strike Force Pearl in its structure?
DC HUDSON: It was similar, sir. I established Shelter. I was the Acting
Commissioner in October 2023, and following the Hamas attack, I considered that
a proactive response was needed to maintain social cohesion, both patrols of Jewish
interests and Islamic interests, a high visibility operation to ensure there was no
escalation of violence on the streets of Sydney.
MR LANCASTER SC: Part of your statement deals with the relationship between
New South Wales Police and the Jewish community, understood broadly, but also
with CSG, the security group.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you first about the relationship with the CSG. In
paragraphs 58 and 59, you acknowledge the important service CSG provides for the
Jewish community in New South Wales?
DC HUDSON: Yes, I do.
MR LANCASTER SC: And I take it from what you have said in the next couple of
paragraphs of your statement, that the role of - you have the view that:
"The role of CSG does not, and should not, supplant or displace the role of the police
in protecting all members of the community, including the Jewish community."
DC HUDSON: Yes, that's my statement, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes, and you identify in your statement that:
"The police would have considerable reservations about granting additional powers
or privileges to CSG in respect of law enforcement."
Could you explain that view?
DC HUDSON: Sir, I think isolating a particular group for additional powers within
our community is problematic. It creates a disconnect between groups. It can cause
friction between groups if one particular element of society is afforded privileges that
others aren't.
MR LANCASTER SC: I can indicate the Commission - and this has been stated
previously - is to have a future Hearing Block in relation to community security for
the Jewish community, but I'm addressing your statement because we have you here
now.

DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you address in paragraph 60 and 61 that the capacity
of New South Wales Police in this regard, the other side of the coin to the
reservations you have expressed is in your view police has sufficient capacity to be
able to allocate resources appropriately if there are enduring threats to the Jewish
community in particular. Is that your evidence?
DC HUDSON: Yes, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you a question about that part of your statement
that deals with information sharing between agencies?
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Your statement addresses a question from the Commission
about whether the New South Wales Police Force recommends any changes to the
current authorising requirement for sharing information between Commonwealth and
State law enforcement security and intelligence agencies.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And your answer in paragraph 20 refers to the PSPF, which
is the Protective Security Policy Framework.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: That regulates the management of information held by
Commonwealth agencies.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, you refer in paragraph 21 to a variety of agreements
and memoranda of understanding between the New South Wales Police Force and
various Commonwealth agencies in relation to information handling and information
sharing.
DC HUDSON: Yes, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: And those arrangements are, as you explain, for
information that's classified, protected or restricted under that framework.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Could you address the topic in paragraph 53, that is, what
has the police observation been about the nature of information sharing over the
time, just at a general level?

DC HUDSON: Which paragraph, sorry, sir?
MS CALLAN SC: It's 23.
MR LANCASTER SC: I said 53, I'm sorry. 23.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: So what have you observed about the information sharing
arrangements in their operation?
DC HUDSON: In my - I had observed different agencies having different
interpretations of the PSPF in relation to what is allowed to be shared between
agencies. From our perspective, we take a very open interpretation of the PSPF and if
there is risk or threat, we will share information with other agencies. But other
agencies can, on occasions, not be so forthcoming.
MR LANCASTER SC: And has that created a difficulty in dealing with other
agencies in terms of the relationship with information sharing?
DC HUDSON: On occasions. We work through the cases on individual bases, but
security classifications around information, getting information to the areas where it
needs to be, in my opinion, should be the priority to be appropriately addressed,
rather than relying upon the PSPF and as a justification for not sharing information.
COMMISSIONER: Deputy Commissioner, you may have already said this but the
PSPF is the Protective Security Policy Framework; is that right?
DC HUDSON: Yes, Commissioner, I apologise.
MR LANCASTER SC: You referred to there being some differences of opinion in
the interpretation of the framework; is that right?
DC HUDSON: That's correct, yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you hold the view, do you, that there should be
a review of the framework?
DC HUDSON: So I think there needs to be consistency across agencies in its
application. And if that - a review is required for that, then, yes, I would suggest
there should be a review.
MR LANCASTER SC: So whether or not that sounds in any different expression of
the obligations of sharing, it will at least get the agencies on the same page in terms
of interpretation and application.

DC HUDSON: Yes, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you about a more recent operation announced in
respect of New South Wales Policing, which is the permanent Rapid Response Team
that you deal with in paragraph 36 and following.
DC HUDSON: Yes, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Why was a permanent Rapid Response Team announced?
DC HUDSON: It was a discussion, I believe, between the Commissioner and
government following the attack on Bondi but also - and obviously relevant to
that - in relation to our capabilities, our current capabilities, and what they needed to
be, moving forward. We have a limited long arm capability within our organisation,
at the moment confined to the Tactical Operations Group and the Public Order &
Riot Squad. The Public Order & Riot Squad received long arms in 2017. And the
current environment, what happened at Bondi and the current environment in relation
to organised crime caused discussions in relation to what our capability needed to be
moving forward.
MR LANCASTER SC: There were, before December last year, limited
circumstances in which police had long arm weapon capability or possession when
they were tasked for a particular purpose? Is that right?
DC HUDSON: Yes, sir. Different thresholds for the Tactical Operations Group. It
was a region Commander, Assistant Commissioner level, who approved special
weapons and tactics to resolve a specific situation. And for the Public Order & Riot
Squad, it was a Deputy Commissioner could forward deploy long arms and the
Commissioner had to approve their open sling of those weapons at an event or in
public.
MR LANCASTER SC: And this Rapid Response Team that I think is to be known
as the Armed Response Command, is that going to operate similarly or differently to
those other commands that you have referred to that have a current capacity for use
of long arms?
DC HUDSON: The use of long arms will change across the organisation.
Deployment of long arms visibly will be a decision by the Commander in the Public
Order & Riot Squad, not the Commissioner. It will still be a decision for an Assistant
Commissioner to approve special weapons and tactics for a specific situation, with
the Tactical Operations Group, but the Armed Response Command will have access
to their weapons when they are on patrol.
MR LANCASTER SC: And is it expected that that new Armed Response
Command team will be in a position to respond differently or more rapidly than on
current capability, for example, the Riot Squad or the TIU?

DC HUDSON: The resources of the Riot Squad are limited and they have
multifunctions. Their main purpose of their creation was public order issues, and
once they are slinging a long arm, they are no longer allowed to engage in riot
control because of - if they need to get hands on with an individual, they can't have
the long arm for safety reasons. So it does limit that capability. So they have been
used sparingly in that capacity. The Armed Response Command will have dual
purpose. It will be high visibility operations, both static and mobile, similar to
models that we have seen overseas about how they are deployed, both in a static
mode, potentially, at events, but also a roving permission commanded by 24/7 Police
Operations Centre which will track where those Armed Response Units are and what
capabilities are on the streets 24/7.
MR LANCASTER SC: Does the creation of this Armed Response Command
involve any sort of acknowledgement that what previously existed was insufficient in
some way, or perhaps I could put an alternative explanation that Assistant
Commissioner McKenna said yesterday, which is just it's a new world since 14
December 2025 in New South Wales?
DC HUDSON: I think the environment has changed for us, but it's not just the
deployment of the Armed Response Command to events, static, patrolling.
Obviously, on 14 December our police officers were placed at significant risk, being
in a gun fight armed with 9-millimetre Glocks against long arms. There has been,
obviously, on behalf of officers within the New South Wales Police Force
representations made by the Police Association of New South Wales, their union, in
relation to what capability increases can better protect them as well, their officers,
their members; the availability of long arms on a more frequent basis is certainly
a response to that and also better protection of the community. So it's two-fold.
MR LANCASTER SC: The title of the new command, Armed Response
Command, suggests that it will be responsive to incidents, but is it intended that that
would also be deployed proactively? In other words, to address an upcoming event
rather than just being responsive to an incident?
DC HUDSON: Both, sir. They will do static guards or static presence at events, but
they will also do mobile patrolling within certain sectors monitored through a Police
Operations Centre to ensure appropriate coverage over the most required areas.
Incrementally, the Armed Response Command will replace the responsibility of
Shelter, which is currently in operation, and become a permanent fixture rather than
a surge capability that Shelter has become.
MR LANCASTER SC: And you indicated in your statement it will compromise
250 additional positions. So the command itself will be comprised of those 250 or
is - did you mean that suggest it will be 250 additional to something else?
DC HUDSON: 250 will be the strength of that command. The frontline presence
plus the command structure plus intelligence officers which will be deployed to that
unit to ensure they are deployed appropriately.

MR LANCASTER SC: You indicate an expectation on the part of the force that
formation of new command will take between 18 months and two years.
DC HUDSON: Potentially less than that, sir.
MR LANCASTER SC: Why that sort of time period?
DC HUDSON: There is a training regime that's required for training of police in
long arm capabilities. At the moment we have trained our weapons trainers in long
arm training. That has been taught by the Public Order & Riot Squad trainers and the
Tactical Operations Group trainers to our general weapons practitioners. So there's
a number of those officers being trained at the moment so they can train the greater
cohort.
Once an individual is selected or identified for a position within the Armed Response
Command, there's a minimum of 10 days training and familiarisation with a long
arm, plus the tactics involved in that, especially integration with active armed
offender training and how a long arm deployed to an environment which is currently
where there is activity with general duties police, armed with a Glock and how that
intra-operability interacts. There's a lot of training in relation to that.
So it's expected that incrementally, probably at 50 individuals per graduation class,
that can backfill the places that these officers will come from, that that command will
be built, probably over the next 12 months now. We have escalated that process. And
as that command is built, Shelter will reduce the responsibilities or Shelter will
reduce as those responsibilities are taken up by the Armed Response Command.
COMMISSIONER: When the Armed Response Command is at full strength, how
many armed frontline officers do you expect it will have?
DC HUDSON: In excess of - just in the Armed Response Command?
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
DC HUDSON: 210, I think the numbers are at the moment.
COMMISSIONER: And they will have a number of vehicles so that the command
could have resources, that is, frontline police officers with long arms, at several
events or incidents?
DC HUDSON: Depending on the risk framework and the threat assessments
conducted of different events, yes, that's correct, Commissioner.
MR LANCASTER SC: Can I ask you now, Deputy Commissioner, about your
response to a question about the effectiveness of the National Counter Terrorism

Framework and, in particular, the management of risks posed by persons who have
come to the attention of intelligence or law enforcement in the past.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Part of your statement deals with that and refers to the
Known Entity Management model that's applied.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
MR LANCASTER SC: Now, it's right, is it, that any person who has come to the
attention of intelligence and law enforcement agencies in respect of terrorism at
some point in the past, as you say in your statement, but is not currently under active
investigation or monitoring, is placed on this Known Entity Management model list?
DC HUDSON: In New South Wales, sir, yes. I can't say for other states.
MR LANCASTER SC: Yes. And there are various tiers of that model, according to
the nature of the individual concerned?
DC HUDSON: That's correct, sir. There are four tiers.
MR LANCASTER SC: And what's your view about the effectiveness of a Known
Entity Management model or policing in respect of counter terrorism?
DC HUDSON: Prior to the creation of the Known Entity Management model, there
was no way of retaining information in relation to specific people of interest to us
that had been of interest to us previously. I think a constant assessment of
individuals, certainly in the first three tiers as to what their current activities are,
what their current personal situations are and whether they are likely to be
problematic to us as individuals is certainly valuable.
I was instrumental in the development of the Known Entity Management model in
2017 based on occurrences that had historically occurred in New South Wales but
also around the world of individuals who had previously come under the notice of
counter terrorism police, had been discarded as appropriate suspects, but there were
obviously some residual risk as they had gone on to commit offences.
So within my jurisdiction, I discussed with the Commander of the Counter Terrorism
Command what I referred to as residual risk of these individuals and how that was to
be captured and monitored.
MR LANCASTER SC: So if an individual comes to the attention of New South
Wales authorities in respect of terrorism or suspected terrorism and is placed on the
list at one or other of the four tiers, what, in broad terms, then would occur under the
model if there's new information about that person that comes to light subsequently?

DC HUDSON: There'd be a reassessment of that individual based on the
information that came in under the notice of police, came to the notice of police, to
see whether they were worthy of additional activity, investigative activity, by us.
MR LANCASTER SC: Thanks, Deputy Commissioner, I don't have any further
questions.
COMMISSIONER: Deputy Commissioner, can I just ask you a few questions about
Operation Shelter.
DC HUDSON: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: To see if I've got it right. On 11 October 2023, after the Hamas
attack on Israel, you perceived the need for additional resources to provide protection
to the Jewish community.
DC HUDSON: Commissioner, not just the Jewish community but reprisals against
the Islamic community as well.
COMMISSIONER: I see.
DC HUDSON: So some of the taskings were certainly committed towards places of
worship of - for the Islamic community as well.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. And at that time, do I take it that Operation Shelter had
a number of police officers attached to it with taskings that related to protection of
those communities?
DC HUDSON: Yes, Commissioner. It was a surge capability. The resources were
obtained from other commands and temporarily seconded to Operation Shelter under
the direction initially of Assistant Commissioner Scott Whyte.
COMMISSIONER: So Operation Shelter was a police operation that had the
capacity to surge resources from other commands when it was considered necessary
for the protection of the Jewish community and the Islamic community, but would it
be right to say at times that capacity reduced to nil?
DC HUDSON: Not initially, Commissioner. When we initially established it, I think
there was over 200 shifts per day.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
DC HUDSON: Were allocated that Shelter had to attend certain taskings, certain
places of interest of both the Jewish and Islamic communities.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.

DC HUDSON: Plus patrolling other sites based on intelligence. And intelligence
what - that was coming into Operation Shelter - it had an intelligence capability as
well - it was also important for us to document and record all those interactions and
taskings which were certainly done through spreadsheets maintained by
operational - by Operation Shelter at the Police Operations Command.
COMMISSIONER: As I understand it, after the arrest of those individuals charged
with offences by Operation Pearl, it appeared that the incidents of violent attacks on
buildings within the Jewish community reduced notably. Is that so?
DC HUDSON: Yes, Commissioner. It was identified through investigations that
those incidents had been orchestrated by a limited number of people, upon direction
of others, and once we went to resolution phase on those individuals, those highly
brazen attacks disappeared.
COMMISSIONER: So that what was the position by mid-December 2025? Was
Operation Shelter active? Did it have many police resources attached to it or not?
DC HUDSON: Operation Shelter was under the direction of Field Operations, not
my area.
COMMISSIONER: I see.
DC HUDSON: But I know that the response was absorbed by the Central
Metropolitan Region for the management of protests and any proactive taskings that
fell to Central Metropolitan Region, rather than a centralised group where resources
were taken from other commands to staff it.
COMMISSIONER: So that, in effect, Operation Shelter, at that time, was no longer
functioning?
DC HUDSON: In name only as a capture process, I believe, for reports, and certain
deployments at local level by commands, but not a centralised group that was
deployed centrally across Sydney.
COMMISSIONER: And since the attack on Bondi, has Operation Shelter been
reinvigorated, if I can put it that way?
DC HUDSON: Certainly, Commissioner. It's been in effect since very shortly after
14 December.
COMMISSIONER: And the intention is that will remain an active policing
resource until the Armed Response Command becomes operational?
DC HUDSON: That's correct, Commissioner. As I indicated, the Armed Response
Command will be built incrementally, probably at 50 officers per attestation class at
this stage. Next year, there are four classes. There's two more classes this year. So
